name: Wei Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers or AI firms; your individual answers are confidential. Could you walk me through a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Wei Diaz, 27, a senior operator at a large mine. I check the haul truck at the start of shift, lead the crew through the pit route, then finish the handover notes before I go home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing my crew trusts me when the road or equipment changes. The long noise and dust wear me down, and the notes at the end of a twelve-hour shift can feel endless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a faster report is handy, but the mine still needs people who know the sound of a machine under load. At dinner I’d say the change looks small from where I sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m a lead operator, so I already use a screen for dispatch notes, but the haul truck and the road conditions still demand judgement. My pay and savings give me room to watch without pretending nothing can go wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my current roster and put a little more into my savings each payday. I’d try the mine’s report assistant on a low-risk shift after a supervisor explains its limits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly **steady**, with a little curiosity about the new tool. The long shifts and safety checks still tire me more than software does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your shift would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might spend less time writing handover notes, especially after a routine shift. I’d still walk the equipment with the crew before signing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone close to you that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my brother that I’m not changing careers over a tool that saves a few minutes. I’d show him the machine logs before trusting a generated summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that planning software could cut some desk work, while the pit still needs experienced operators. I wouldn’t promise that every job stays as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work is mostly hands-on, but I do route planning and incident notes, and those parts could shrink first. I expect a gradual change, and my local options and savings give me some control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the approved dispatch features this year and ask the safety lead to review any AI-written incident note. If hiring slows, I’d talk to two nearby mines before the next roster cycle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m **uneasy**, not frightened, because the screens may change before the machine work does. I’d miss teaching new operators if there were fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your shift would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want to know whether the system can see a wet haul road after a storm. The shift boss would still need a person to check the ground and stop a truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone close to you that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner that I can learn a new console, but I won’t sign a safety report I haven’t checked. I’d use the next toolbox meeting to ask who owns that decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my crew that AGI could take the planning desk quickly, but the robots are not due in the pit until 2031. I’d ask management for a clear safety plan before anyone treats the dates as certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If machines can do every thinking task by 2028, the dispatch and reporting parts of my role are exposed even though I operate trucks. I could lose some hours, but my strong savings and nearby mines make a sudden household crisis less likely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for cross-training on maintenance checks now and apply to two local operations roles by next spring if dispatch work disappears. In 2028 I’d follow the mine’s transition plan, while keeping a separate emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels **short**, and I’d think hard about whether I want to spend my twenties waiting for robot trucks. I still believe practical skill and a clean safety record count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your shift would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The route assignments and incident notes would change before I stopped driving. I’d still check the haul road myself, but I could lose paid planning hours once the system handles those jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone close to you that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my younger cousin that a technical diploma helped me, but no diploma makes a person untouchable. I’d train beside the equipment now and keep my options open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell people that five years gives a mine time to plan, if leaders use it well. I would want the crew told early if the dispatch office is being reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full thinking AI by 2031 could remove my planning and paperwork tasks before the robots arrive in 2034. I expect the equipment work to last longer, but I can’t call it permanent protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d complete a maintenance course over the next two years and keep my current team lead duties while they remain. If the mine announces cuts in 2031, I’d apply to the neighboring sites immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel **anxious** about the thinking side, though five years lets me act. I’d rather make a move while I’m still young than wait for a robot announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your shift would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the mine manager for a written skills map showing which crew roles remain after 2031. My savings would let me take a short period between jobs, but I’d rather keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone close to you that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner that I can study while working and that we should hold off on a larger home purchase. I don’t want a long warning to become an excuse for doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a decade is enough time to learn and plan, but not a guarantee that the mine will keep our current jobs. I’d ask for yearly updates instead of one late announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036, full thinking AI could take my dispatch planning, and robots follow around 2039 for the machine work. My income could fall before then, so I’d use the years to build a second set of skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d finish maintenance training over the next three years and save more from each bonus. In 2036 I’d move into a hands-on maintenance opening if one is available, then reassess before robot deployment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes me **hopeful**, but the robot date still sits in the back of my mind. I don’t want to be 37 and only then start asking what else I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your shift would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d review my skills every year with the training coordinator and keep records of the machines I’ve handled. I’d also ask whether the mine will fund practical certificates for operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell someone close to you that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my partner that we can make family plans without assuming my mine pay lasts forever. I’d rather save steadily now than make a panic decision at the end.

I need **maintenance skills** before my mine income falls.

Save more from each **work bonus** before 2036.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the dispatch work could go before the robots arrive. Paid maintenance training and a clear schedule from mine management would help me act while I still have choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d ask whether operators can see the actual skills plan before cuts are announced. I can handle change better when the rules are clear and the training is practical.

headlineQuote: The long noise and dust wear me down, and the notes at the end of a twelve-hour shift can feel endless.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old** senior mine operator with a technical diploma and a strong savings cushion.
He values **field judgement** and crew trust, while accepting useful technology after it is proven.
He expects **planning and reports** to change before robots reach his equipment work.
His **savings and nearby mines** let him pursue maintenance training and other roles while he keeps earning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because dispatch work could vanish before robots arrive, leaving little time to change roles.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid maintenance training** and a clear schedule from mine management would help him act while he has choices.
